blocks.heading: Why classify and measure businesses?
blocks.text: Classification groups businesses by a shared characteristic, such as activity sector or ownership. Measurement indicates scale through an appropriate size indicator. Governments can use sector and employment information to identify where support or infrastructure may be needed. A lender can compare an applicant with businesses of similar activity and scale instead of interpreting its turnover without context. Managers can monitor changes over time and compare competitors. Investors may use size data as background, but size alone cannot establish return or safety. A classification is useful only if its categories fit the question. Primary/secondary/tertiary helps describe economic activity; public/private helps describe ownership. Neither directly ranks business size. Measurement must also be consistent: compare annual turnover over the same length of time and avoid comparing one firm’s sales revenue with another’s profit. Two businesses may be similar in employment but different in assets, so describe that result instead of forcing a single ranking. The purpose of the decision determines the most useful classification and measure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A local planning office needs to assess employment opportunities in food processing. It receives employment totals for food factories and sales totals for farms. Food processing is secondary while farming is primary. The office should obtain comparable employment figures for the relevant processors before judging their job contribution. Farm turnover cannot be treated as the missing factory employee count.
